Guided trip

Travel to exoplanets

Other stars' planets, then TRAPPIST-1's seven. Leaving brings you back to Earth.

Open the trip: Travel to exoplanets

Planets around other stars

6 423 planets around other stars, in the copy of NASA's catalogue this map carries, each drawn as a mark at its star. Most were found by the dip in a star's light as a planet crosses in front of it, the rest mostly by the wobble a planet gives its star.

The nearest one

Proxima b goes round the nearest star to the Sun, four light-years away, once every eleven days. Nobody has seen it: it was found by the wobble it gives its star.

Seven worlds round a small red star

TRAPPIST-1 is a cool red star forty light-years away, a little bigger than Jupiter. Seven planets about the size of the Earth go round it, and all seven were found as they crossed in front of it.

TRAPPIST-1 e

A year here lasts six days. It is nine tenths as wide as the Earth and seven tenths as heavy, and at its closest its neighbour d would look as wide in its sky as the Moon is in ours.

TRAPPIST-1 b

The innermost, 1.7 million kilometres from its star, over thirty times closer than Mercury is to the Sun. Its year is a day and a half, and it is a tenth wider than the Earth.

TRAPPIST-1 c

The second out, round its star in just under two and a half days. Like b it is a little wider than the Earth and about a third heavier.

TRAPPIST-1 d

Four days a year, and the smallest but one: four fifths of the Earth's width and less than two fifths of its mass.

TRAPPIST-1 f

Nine days a year, and the nearest of the seven to the Earth's own size and mass, a few per cent over on both.

TRAPPIST-1 g

The widest of the seven, thirteen per cent wider than the Earth. Its year lasts twelve and a third days.

TRAPPIST-1 h

The outermost and the smallest, three quarters of the Earth's width. A year here is nineteen days, and b goes round twelve times in one of them.

All of it inside Mercury's orbit

The dashed ring is the size of Mercury's orbit round our Sun, drawn here for scale. It is six times wider than the orbit of h: every one of these worlds is closer to its star than Mercury is to ours.

Everything is drawn where it really is, from the HYG star database, the NASA Exoplanet Archive and the planets’ own orbits (astronomy-engine).
